passage: From the window of my flat I can see the nursery school's courtyard, and every morning I watch Aadhya, five, walk in and go straight to the bench where Ira waits. Aadhya sits so close their sleeves touch, and swings her legs in time with Ira's. Today, though, after a quarrel over the red bucket, Aadhya sat at the far end of the bench, looking at the sand. By lunch she had shuffled back next to Ira. I can't say what they said to each other.

qa.q: Where does Aadhya go every morning?
qa.a: She goes straight to the bench where Ira waits.

qa.q: What might Aadhya's choice of seats say about how she felt today?
qa.a: Sitting at the far end after the quarrel suggests she was upset with Ira, and shuffling back by lunch suggests the quarrel had eased. Kids also move seats for fun, so it's only a guess.

qa.q: What could an adult watching do if a child keeps sitting apart from a friend?
qa.a: She can watch the pattern over several days before deciding anything, and stay ready to help if the child seems upset.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Aadhya sits at the far end?
qa.a: She may feel unsure or a little hurt, and glad when Aadhya returns to sit beside her.

grounding: Sitting close shows liking and comfort, while shifting away can show a quarrel, seen by an observer who can only guess.

passage:
Day one: at the Bristol nursery, Jyoti, five, walked into the reading corner and sat down right next to Rehana. Their knees touched as they looked at the same book.
Day three: Jyoti chose the beanbag across the room and pulled out a puzzle. Rehana didn't say anything but went to the shelf by herself.
Day five: after a shared snack, Jyoti dragged her cushion beside Rehana again and whispered, "Can I see your page?" Rehana shifted over to make space.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do on day five to sit next to Rehana?
qa.a: She dragged her cushion beside Rehana.

qa.q: What might Jyoti's move to the beanbag on day three suggest, and what does the pattern of days add?
qa.a: The move might mean a quarrel or a wish to be apart, but she chose the puzzle, so it might just have been for fun. Coming back to sit close on day five suggests she still likes Rehana.

qa.q: What could the teacher do if a child keeps changing seats?
qa.a: She can watch the pattern over several days, and check in gently if a child seems left out or upset.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel when Jyoti sits beside her again?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and reassured, since she moved over to make space.

grounding: Choosing a seat beside a friend shows liking and comfort, and patterns across days matter more than one moment.

passage:
Day one: at the tea stall in Patna, Sudha, four, dropped a spoon and her father Tanvir caught it before it hit the floor. She let out a low, pleased chortle. "Again!" He tossed it, caught it and she gurgled deeper.
Day three: Tanvir did a silly walk to the door and Sudha chortled at him, hand over her mouth.
Day six: Sudha herself dropped a spoon for her mother to catch, watching her face and chuckling in the same low way as her father.

qa.q: What did Sudha drop at the tea stall on day one?
qa.a: She dropped a spoon.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she chortled on day three?
qa.a: She was pleased and amused by her father's silly walk, and she covered her mouth with her hand. She may also have been enjoying the fun of sharing a game.

qa.q: What might Tanvir do to keep sharing this fun with Sudha?
qa.a: He can keep playing simple games she enjoys and laugh along with her.

qa.q: How might Sudha's mother feel when Sudha drops the spoon for her to catch?
qa.a: She may feel delighted to be part of the game, and notice that Sudha's chuckle sounds just like her father's.

grounding: A young child chortles with pleased delight when a game works, and copies the laughter style of the adults around her.

passage: The bus was stuck in a mud-slick lane after the rains near Pune, and Urmila, five, had been kept waiting so long her legs were restless. Her uncle Darshan pulled a crumpled paper hat from his pocket and put it on his head. Urmila glanced at him and let out a low chuckle that shook her shoulders. "Uncle, it's tiny!" He wiggled his ears. She gave a deep chortle, eyes shining, and the other passengers turned round and smiled. She pointed at the hat, waiting for more.

qa.q: What did Darshan take from his pocket?
qa.a: He took a crumpled paper hat from his pocket.

qa.q: What does Urmila's chuckle suggest she was feeling about the hat?
qa.a: It suggests she was amused and delighted, since her eyes were shining and she pointed at the hat for more. The wait may also have made her glad of any distraction.

qa.q: What could Darshan do next if the wait goes on?
qa.a: He can invent another small silly game, since it changed the mood for Urmila.

qa.q: How might the other passengers feel seeing this?
qa.a: They may feel warmed by Urmila's laughter, since they turned round and smiled.

grounding: A young child gives a low, pleased chortle when a joke or surprise works, showing shared enjoyment.

passage: At the Delhi birthday party, Charu, five, said "poo-poo pudding" and burst into giggles. Rekha, at the next table, giggled too, and the two of them fell across their chairs with laughter, hands on tummies. Other children joined in, shouting silly words. Charu's mother Kavita walked over and said, "That's a lot of funny words!" Then the cake was cut, and the children went quiet as the candles were blown out. Charu bit her lip, and let out a small nervous giggle, and Rekha leaned against her shoulder.

qa.q: What silly words did Charu say at the party?
qa.a: She said "poo-poo pudding".

qa.q: What might Charu's small giggle at the candles suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She may have been nervous or excited in the sudden quiet, since she bit her lip first. It could also be that the giggle was left over from the earlier fun.

qa.q: What could Charu's mother do about the silly words?
qa.a: She can join the fun for a moment and gently remind the children to keep the party's calm times respectful.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Charu's giggle when the room is quiet?
qa.a: She may find it catching or comforting, since she leaned on Charu's shoulder.

grounding: A preschooler giggles at silly words with peers, and giggling in a serious moment can be nerves and not disrespect.

passage:
"Baljeet, say 'bum'!"
"Bum!"
Lokesh doubled over. "Bum, bum, bum!"
"Shh!" Baljeet wheezed. Both of them were red in the face, laughing.
Their teacher was coming. Lokesh clamped a hand over his mouth. "She's coming."
"Stop laughing!"
"I can't!"
The teacher stopped at their table. "What's so funny?" Baljeet whispered, "Nothing." Lokesh let out a squeak of laughter. The teacher hid her own smile.

qa.q: What word did Lokesh ask Baljeet to say?
qa.a: He asked Baljeet to say "bum".

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he clamped his hand over his mouth?
qa.a: He was trying to stop laughing because the teacher was coming, though the giggles kept coming out. He was probably excited and a little worried about being caught.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next?
qa.a: She can let the giggles out later, such as at a break, and ask the boys to save the silly words for playtime.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel when Lokesh squeaks?
qa.a: She may find it funny herself, since she hid her own smile, while knowing she should stay calm.

grounding: Preschool giggles spread quickly and can come out even when a child tries to stop, showing joy and belonging.

passage: In the quiet room of a Hamburg school, the teacher was reading a story about a sleepy bear. Oskar, six, heard the bear snore loudly in the story and pressed his lips together. His eyes darted to Sofia, who bit her lip. He looked down at his shoes and his shoulders shook. He covered his mouth with his hand. When the teacher turned the page, a small squeak escaped, and both of them looked at each other, then away. At break they ran outside and let out a big roar of laughter.

qa.q: What was the teacher reading about?
qa.a: She was reading a story about a sleepy bear.

qa.q: What might Oskar have been feeling as he pressed his lips together and looked down?
qa.a: He seems to have been fighting a giggle and knew it was a quiet time, so he tried to control himself. He might also have felt a bit nervous about being noticed.

qa.q: How could a teacher help children who get the giggles in a quiet moment?
qa.a: She can give a short movement break, or let them share the joke in a whisper later.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel while trying not to laugh?
qa.a: She may feel the same struggle as Oskar, and biting her lip shows she is also trying to hold back.

grounding: A child holds back a giggle in a quiet moment, showing awareness of rules and effort at self-control.

passage: Assembly at the Bhubaneswar school hall was silent when the head teacher's phone rang with a loud duck-quack tune. Pema, five, felt her chest bounce and pressed her lips together, staring hard at the floor. Beside her, Ira covered her mouth with both hands, shoulders shaking. The head teacher looked embarrassed, and the whole hall held its breath. Pema pinched her own arm gently. Ira let out one small snort, and looked terrified. As the children left the hall, the two girls ran ahead and burst into laughter.

qa.q: What sound did the head teacher's phone make?
qa.a: It rang with a loud duck-quack tune.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling as she covered her mouth and looked terrified?
qa.a: She was fighting a strong urge to laugh and was afraid of getting into trouble after the snort. She may also have felt embarrassed.

qa.q: What would help the girls the next time they get the giggles in a quiet place?
qa.a: A short movement break or a chance to laugh once they are outside would help them release it.

qa.q: How might the head teacher feel about the silence in the hall?
qa.a: She may feel embarrassed about the phone, and the children's effort to stay quiet may even ease her embarrassment.

grounding: A child holds back giggles in assembly, showing rule awareness and self-control, and releases it later.

passage: After the village fair in Bikaner, Ojas, five, threw himself on the ground because his father Trisha had said no to a fourth balloon. He screamed, kicking, and dust rose. Trisha squatted beside him, hands loose, not speaking. When the screaming eased, Ojas sobbed, "You said... you said I could have it... at the start!" Trisha said, "You're sad and cross because you wanted more. The balloons are finished for today, but we can walk to see the camels." Ojas wiped his nose and, still hiccuping, took his father's hand.

qa.q: Why did Ojas throw himself on the ground?
qa.a: His father had said no to a fourth balloon.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he cried and explained what went wrong?
qa.a: He felt sad and cross because he wanted another balloon, and he thought he was told he could have it. Feelings this big can outrun his words.

qa.q: What did Trisha do that worked well?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named the feeling and set a kind limit with the offer of camels, without punishing the tears.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel when his father squats beside him and doesn't speak?
qa.a: He may feel less alone and less afraid, since his father was close.

grounding: A preschooler wails in a tantrum then cries while explaining, and a calm adult names the feeling and sets a kind limit.

passage: In their kitchen in Enugu, Chidi, four, wailed when his older sister Paulo took the last biscuit. His face was red and tears rolled. "It's mine!" Paulo froze. Their father knelt down. "You're really upset." Chidi kept crying, then said, wetly, "She always... gets the big one." "So you feel it's unfair," said their father. "We can fix it. You're going to choose which biscuit you'd like tomorrow, first." Chidi sniffed. "Promise?" Their father nodded.

qa.q: What did Paulo take?
qa.a: Paulo took the last biscuit.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling when he said "She always... gets the big one"?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair and was hurt and angry. The words came out while he was still crying, so he was probably still very upset.

qa.q: What could their father do next to help both children?
qa.a: He can keep his promise about choosing first and make sure Paulo also feels heard.

qa.q: How might Paulo feel after freezing and hearing Chidi?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and a little guilty, and may want to make it right.

grounding: A preschooler wails then cries while explaining what went wrong, and a calm adult names the emotion and offers a fix.

subtype: Learning it is okay to cry [Regulating]
passage:
"Stop crying, Vaibhav! Be brave!" said Uncle Nikhil at the door of the flat, while Vaibhav, five, sobbed over a torn kite. His mother Indu came in, knelt and said, "It's okay to cry. It's really sad when a kite tears."
Vaibhav sniffed. "I made it myself."
"I know. Come here." She held him for a moment, then asked, "Shall we tell Nani what happened?" "Yes." "And tomorrow we could stick it back together." He wiped his face and nodded.

qa.q: What had torn?
qa.a: Vaibhav's kite had torn.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he said "I made it myself"?
qa.a: He was sad because the kite was something he had worked on, and the tear felt like a real loss. He might also have felt his uncle's words as pressure to hide it.

qa.q: What worked in Indu's response?
qa.a: She said crying was okay, comforted him and then talked about what happened and how to fix it.

qa.q: How might Uncle Nikhil see Vaibhav's crying?
qa.a: He may feel uncomfortable and want to make it stop, without realising that telling Vaibhav to be brave might teach him to hide feelings.

grounding: A child told to be brave may hide feelings, while hearing it's okay to cry helps him handle sadness.

subtype: Learning it is okay to cry [Regulating]
passage: Nursery note by Rajni, Class 1 teacher. At pick-up, Jasleen, five, began to cry when her friend left with another girl. The child's aunt said, "Don't cry, be a big girl." Jasleen wiped her eyes hard and went silent. I stayed near her and said, "It's okay to cry, Jasleen. It hurts when a friend leaves." She cried more openly then, and when she was calmer, she said, "I wanted her to stay with me." We talked about asking her friend to play tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the aunt say to Jasleen?
qa.a: She said, "Don't cry, be a big girl."

qa.q: What might Jasleen have felt when she wiped her eyes hard and went silent?
qa.a: She may have felt she was not allowed to be sad, so she tried to hide her feelings. Underneath she was still hurt that her friend left.

qa.q: What could Rajni do to support Jasleen tomorrow?
qa.a: She can help Jasleen ask her friend to play, and keep letting her know that feelings are welcome.

qa.q: How might the aunt see Jasleen's crying?
qa.a: She may think she is helping by telling Jasleen to be big, though this may teach Jasleen to hide her feelings.

grounding: A child told not to cry hides feelings, while comfort and a talk about what happened builds emotional skills.

passage: On the swing set in a park in Accra, Kwame, five, went higher than ever and whooped, both hands raised. "Look at me, Rania!" he shouted. His cousin Rania, waiting her turn, cheered and squealed too. Then they walked past the small clinic at the park's edge. Kwame started to whoop again, but Rania put a finger on her lips. "Shh, people are resting." He lowered his voice to a whisper, "Whee." As they reached the grass, they both let out a big shout.

qa.q: Where did Kwame whoop?
qa.a: He whooped on the swing set in a park in Accra.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling as he swung higher and shouted?
qa.a: He felt joy and excitement at going higher than ever. It was a welcome noise in play, though he had to learn to notice other settings.

qa.q: What could an adult do to help Kwame read settings?
qa.a: She can tell him ahead of time that a clinic is a quiet place and use a signal, like a finger to the lips, as Rania did.

qa.q: How might a person resting near the clinic feel about Kwame's whooping?
qa.a: They may feel disturbed, so it matters that Kwame lowered his voice near the clinic.

grounding: A preschooler cheers and whoops for joy, and reading settings such as a quiet clinic is a skill still being learned.

passage: In the waiting room of a hospital in Hyderabad, Tejas, five, saw a fish tank and squealed, "Wow, fish!" Hrithik, the nurse, put a finger on his lips and smiled. Tejas put his hand on his mouth and giggled. Hrithik knelt. "Fish are so cool, aren't they? Here we use small voices. Outside, you can cheer." Tejas whispered, "Small voice." Later, when the doctor said his sister was fine, Tejas hopped and pumped his fists silently, grinning in the corridor and cheering softly.

qa.q: What did Tejas see in the waiting room?
qa.a: He saw a fish tank.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he squealed "Wow, fish!"?
qa.a: He was excited and surprised by the fish. He had not yet realised that a hospital is a place for quiet voices.

qa.q: What worked in the way Hrithik corrected Tejas?
qa.a: He smiled, agreed the fish were cool and explained where to use small voices and where to cheer.

qa.q: How might other people in the waiting room feel about Tejas's squeal?
qa.a: Some may smile, and some who are worried or unwell may feel disturbed, which is why a small voice helps.

grounding: A preschooler squeals with excitement, and learning to read the setting, like a hospital, takes gentle reminders.

passage:
Day one: at their Ranchi flat, Leela, five, shouted "I want juice!" across the hall. Her mother Seema said, "Indoor voice, please, Leela," and she whispered, "I want juice." Seema said, "Thank you, well tried."
Day three: Leela shouted again but caught herself. "Sorry, indoor voice. Juice, please."
Day six: at the playground she screamed with joy on the slide, and Seema said, "That's your outdoor voice, perfect." At home, they made a small picture card with a mouth.

qa.q: What did Leela shout on day one?
qa.a: She shouted, "I want juice!" across the hall.

qa.q: What might Leela have been feeling when she caught herself on day three?
qa.a: She probably wanted juice and got excited, then remembered the reminder and wanted to show she could do it. Her "Sorry" suggests she knew the rule.

qa.q: What helped Leela learn to swap a yell for an indoor voice?
qa.a: Clear reminders, praise for trying and a shared picture card gave her a signal she could use.

qa.q: How might Seema feel as Leela gets better at this?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and patient, since the change is gradual and the card helps both of them.

grounding: A child learns to swap a yell for an indoor voice, and clear rules, praise and a shared signal help self-control grow.

passage: The heavy traffic outside the Toronto clinic drowned out every sound, and Thomas, five, screamed "Chinmay, look, a helicopter!" at his uncle, standing right beside him. Chinmay smiled and touched his ear. "Here, outdoors, that voice is fine. Inside the clinic, use the quiet one." Inside, Thomas remembered, pointed at the card that his uncle had shown him, and whispered, "Shh voice." "Well done," whispered Chinmay. When the nurse called them, Thomas held the card up to show her.

qa.q: What did Thomas see outside the clinic?
qa.a: He saw a helicopter.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he screamed about the helicopter?
qa.a: He was excited and wanted to share it. The traffic was loud, so he may also have thought he needed to shout to be heard.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do to help Thomas use the right voice in future?
qa.a: He can keep using the card and a friendly reminder, and praise Thomas whenever he tries.

qa.q: How might the nurse see Thomas holding up the card?
qa.a: She might find it charming and understand that he is learning to control his voice.

grounding: A child learns to swap a yell for an indoor voice, and a shared signal and praise help.

passage:
"Ready, Lalremsiami? Watch my hand." Shalini closed her fist and opened it slowly to show a coin.
"Ooh!" Lalremsiami gasped and her mouth fell open.
"Where did the coin come from?"
"From your ear!" said Shalini.
Lalremsiami's eyes went round. She gasped again and touched her own ear, her shoulders lifting.
"Do it again!"
Shalini smiled. "Should I make it disappear?"
Lalremsiami squealed and clutched Shalini's sleeve.

qa.q: Where did Shalini say the coin came from?
qa.a: She said it came from Lalremsiami's ear.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami's gasp and round eyes suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest she was amazed and delighted by the trick, since she asked for it again. A gasp only shows a quick intake of attention, so it could also have carried a little surprise or alarm.

qa.q: What could Shalini do to keep the magic fun?
qa.a: She can keep the tricks simple and gentle and check that Lalremsiami stays happy.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel about Lalremsiami's reaction?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and proud that the trick worked, and her smile shows she is enjoying it too.

grounding: A child gasps at a magic trick, showing a quick intake of attention that the face and context read as delight.

passage: Play-group note by Hrithik. During the puppet show, a wolf puppet popped out of the box and Tejas gasped loudly, his hands flying to his cheeks. Was it fear or thrill? His eyes were wide, but he leaned forward and did not move away, and when the wolf spoke he laughed and said, "Again!" A different child in the group also gasped but hid behind her friend, and did not laugh. I checked with her, and she wanted to sit at the back. The gasp alone did not tell me which feeling was there.

qa.q: What popped out of the box?
qa.a: A wolf puppet popped out of the box.

qa.q: What might Tejas's gasp have meant, and what else did the note record?
qa.a: It might have been thrill more than fear, since he leaned forward, laughed and said "Again!" The other child's gasp came with hiding, which suggests alarm.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do for the child who hid?
qa.a: He can let her sit at the back and offer a break, as he checked with her.

qa.q: How might the girl who hid feel when the puppet show goes on?
qa.a: She may feel unsafe until she can be further from the wolf, and her wish to sit at the back shows what she needs.

grounding: A gasp shows a quick intake of attention and only the face and context show whether it is joy or alarm.

passage: I was on the balcony of the next flat when I heard Mridul, five, humming a tune while he drew a boat at the low table. It rose and fell with each pencil stroke. His father Sumit read the paper nearby. Mridul hummed for about ten minutes. Then it stopped. I looked over and Mridul was staring at a pile of dark bills on the table, chewing his pencil. Sumit put down the paper and the humming started again once Sumit said, "Shall we finish the boat?"

qa.q: What was Mridul drawing?
qa.a: He was drawing a boat.

qa.q: What might Mridul have been worrying about when his humming stopped?
qa.a: He might have noticed the bills or felt worried, since he stared at them and chewed his pencil. It could also be that he was concentrating on a hard part.

qa.q: What could Sumit do when the humming stops?
qa.a: He can check gently how Mridul is feeling, as he did by asking about the boat.

qa.q: How might the observer on the balcony see Mridul's humming?
qa.a: She sees a happy child at first, but she can only guess at why it stopped.

grounding: A child hums while drawing from contentment or focus, and a sudden stop may show a change of mood.

passage:
Day one: at their Vizag flat, Nilesh, five, hummed a tune as he built with blocks, and his aunt Tarun smiled, sure he was happy.
Day three: he hummed quietly while waiting outside the dentist, and his humming was tight and fast. Tarun put an arm round him. "Nervous?" He nodded.
Day five: he whistled a wobbly tune while colouring a tree, then stopped when the doorbell rang. "Just the postman," said Tarun. He started to hum again, calmly.

qa.q: What was Nilesh doing on day one while humming?
qa.a: He was building with blocks.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's humming on day three suggest about how he was feeling, and how is it different from day one?
qa.a: On day three it was tight and fast, and he nodded when asked if he was nervous, so the humming was soothing worry. On day one he seemed happy.

qa.q: What could Tarun do to help Nilesh when he hums nervously?
qa.a: She can offer comfort and company and let him hum, as it helps him cope.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel about Tarun asking, "Nervous?"
qa.a: He may feel understood and safe enough to say yes, since he nodded straight away.

grounding: A child hums from contentment or focus, but humming can also soothe worry.
